description: Aspergillus ear rot is an important fungal disease of maize caused mainly by Aspergillus flavus. The disease produces olive-green powdery mold on corn kernels and contaminates grain with aflatoxin, a highly toxic and carcinogenic mycotoxin that threatens livestock and human health and reduces grain marketability.
symptoms: Mold usually begins at the tip of the ear but may spread to the base
Powdery spores disperse like dust when husk is opened
Small ears and stunted plants in dry or stressed areas
Kernel discoloration and reduced seed germination
toxins: Can be present even when kernels appear healthy
disease_cycle: Fungus survives in soil and crop residues as mycelia or sclerotia
Produces conidia (spores) that spread by wind and insects
Infection occurs through silks or wounds caused by insects, birds, or hail
Can infect crops before harvest and remain dormant until storage
Continues producing aflatoxin during hot, dry conditions or delayed harvest
favorable_conditions: High temperature and moisture during storage
monitoring: Inspect at least 30 ears in different field locations before harvest
Peel husks and check for olive-green mold
Focus on dry areas such as sandy soils or hillsides
Monitor stressed plants with small ears
cultural_management: Reduce plant stress through irrigation and proper nutrition
Separate contaminated grain from healthy grain
Remove damaged kernels and maintain sanitation
postharvest_management: Store grain at low temperature (below 5°C when possible)
Use aeration systems in storage bins
biological_control: Pichia anomala yeast competes with Aspergillus flavus and reduces growth up to 97%
Atoxigenic strain Aspergillus flavus AF36 used as biocontrol to reduce aflatoxin production
chemical_or_physical_control: Use fumigants to control insects in storage
Maintain aeration systems to remove heat and moisture
No widely effective fungicide treatments in field conditions
economic_impact: Higher losses possible in developing countries
Major economic losses due to aflatoxin contamination rather than yield reduction
sources: Scientific literature on Aspergillus flavus and aflatoxin contamination
